title: E-ZTax: Tax Salience and Tax Rates
research_question: Does reducing the visibility of a tax to those who pay it lead to higher equilibrium tax rates? Specifically, when payment of a price/tax becomes less perceptible to consumers, do the authorities responsible for setting that rate respond by raising it, and does consumer behavioral responsiveness and the political cost of rate increases also change?
data_description: The author assembled a new panel data set covering 123 publicly owned toll facilities in the United States (roads, bridges, and tunnels, excluding ferries) that were charging tolls in 1985, run by 49 operating authorities across 24 state-level entities. The data include annual histories of nominal passenger-car toll rates (both cash and electronic), the date of electronic toll collection (ETC) adoption (ranging from 1987 through 2005), and, where available, annual facility-level traffic counts (76 facilities), toll revenue (45 facilities), and the share of tolls/revenue paid electronically (about two-thirds of post-ETC facility-years). On average, about 50 years of toll-rate history per facility are observed, with roughly six post-ETC years per adopting facility. Two original surveys of driver toll awareness (a 2007 in-person Massachusetts survey of 214 drivers and a 2004 telephone survey of 362 New Jersey commuters) are also used.
institutional_context: U.S. toll facilities historically collected tolls in cash at plazas, with statutory rate-setting authority vested in toll operating authorities whose boards are appointed by state or local governments, leaving political actors with substantial influence over toll levels. Beginning in the late 1980s, facilities gradually rolled out electronic toll collection systems (e.g., E-ZPass in the Northeast, I-Pass in Illinois, FastTrak in California), which automatically deduct tolls via transponders so drivers no longer count out cash at the booth. Adoption timing varied widely across facilities and authorities, and within adopting facilities the share of tolls paid electronically diffused gradually, reaching a steady state of roughly 60% after about 14 years. Toll changes are infrequent—on average a facility raises its toll only about once a decade—and tend to be smaller in state election years, reflecting political constraints on rate increases. Many adopting authorities also offered modest electronic-payment discounts.
